To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

preweanlings are more likely than adults to encode multimodal stimuli on the basis of stimulus intensity, whereas adults are more likely to attend to the modality-specific properties that distinguish lights from tones.
preweanlings are more likely to select a compound on the basis of its intensity, whereas adults are more likely to respond to its modality.

age-related differences in the selection of stimuli for encoding multimodal compounds in Pavlovian conditioning are due to a shift from encoding on the basis of modality-specific features of stimuli to encoding on the basis, or in the basis, of intensity of the multimodal compound.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ontogeny of stimulus selection in rats.
the development of intersensors, the mechanisms of which are thought to underlie the development of intersensorial function.
the development of intersensORY function in the rat and the mechanisms underlying this development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the development of intersensors function in rats involves a transition from an emphasis on amodal properties of multimodal compounds to a greater emphasis on modality-specific properties.
the preweanling's ability to encode and select multimodal stimuli is less modality specific than that of an adult rat.
the development of intersensorsity function involves the acquisition of the ability to select multimodal compounds on modality-specific bases, rather than on the basis of their intensity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the rat, intersensory function is a developmental process that is completed before the end of the first postnatal month.
the preweanling rat has a greater capacity than the adult for stimulus integration and that this capacity declines with development.

the preweanling rat is more disposed than the adult to encode multimodal stimulus compounds on the basis on amodal intensity, and this difference is reflected in age-related differences in Pavlovian stimulus selection and conditioning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of intersensORY function is an active, experience-driven process that may be influenced by the nature of the stimuli used in early experience.
the age-related differences in the controlling properties that stimuli have on behavior are likely to be due, in large part, to differences in stimulus selection.

age-related changes in intersensory function are more likely to reflect age-related changes in the controlling properties or salience of stimuli than to be a function of age-related changes in stimulus selection.
